> If we make this same origin-domain I think we should just remove the check altogether. It would be
> redundant with https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#integration-with-idl.

It's not redundant in blink, as you don't lose access to objects you once got. So getting the document and the open function, and then setting the document.domain still allows you to call open on the now no longer same origin-domain document. In that case, the check in step 4 triggers.

In Firefox on the other hand, the membrane will revoke access so step 4 might be indeed redundant.

@zcorpan I don't think your tests are correct due to the difference in how security checks are implemented in the two browsers.

@jeisinger it's not redundant in Blink because Blink doesn't implement the "perform a security check" that the HTML standard requires. If we start defining Blink's model, we'd have to remove that check, from HTML and IDL, and define a couple things in a different way. But putting both in would make it logically inconsistent.
@annevk maybe I'm misunderstanding. Can you point me at where "perform a security check" is invoked?
@jeisinger basically for each getter/setter/operation in https://heycam.github.io/webidl/.

the way I read this is that we have to perform the security check when reading the attribute which we do. The result of reading the attribute is converted to a ECMAScript object that doesn't require further access checks.

So something like this is still spec compliant

const doc = window.frames[0].document; // performs access check to get the doc
const docOpen = doc.open.bind(doc); // performs access check to get open from that doc
document.domain = document.domain; // from now on, access checks won't pass anymore
docOpen(); // should be fine.

Thank you, it does indeed seem to only be invoked on creation, not on invocation. So currently HTML describes Chrome's SOP model and not Firefox's model. And this change would add defense-in-depth for `document.open()` matching both.

@bzbarsky does that also match your understanding of things as far as HTML and SOP go?

> @bzbarsky does that also match your understanding of things as far as HTML and SOP go?

Per the current specs as written, in @jeisinger's testcase, when you call `docOpen` you land in the steps defined in step 2 of <https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#dfn-create-operation-function>.  Step 2.1.2.3 says:

>If O is a platform object, then perform a security check, passing O, id, and "method"

which applies to us, since `O` is `doc` in this case.  That drops us in https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#dfn-perform-a-security-check which then calls into <https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#integration-with-idl>.  Step 1 does not apply, but step 2 does, so we land in <https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#isplatformobjectsameorigin-(-o-)>.  But the security check passes, because by this point the "current settings object" is that of the `doc.open` function, which is the same as the relevant settings object of `doc`.

So per current spec as written, this should in fact succeed in calling into the steps of `open`.

On the other hand, doing `document.open.call(doc)` after that `document.domain = document.domain` line should throw per spec, because at that point the current settings object will be that of `document.open` and `O` will be `doc` in <https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#isplatformobjectsameorigin-(-o-)> and the two settings objects are not same origin-domain with each other.

In Gecko the step that would throw in that testcase is crossing the now-revoked membrane to reach the [[Call]] of the `doc.open` function, so none of these steps would be reached at all.  So you're right that the spec does not define Gecko's security model.

On the other hand, Chrome does not seem to perform any security check from inside the IDL operation at all, so the spec also does not define Chrome's security model.  ;)

Moving right along....

> const docOpen = doc.open.bind(doc); // performs access check to get open from that doc

This step does not perform any security checks I'm aware of per the HTML and IDL specs (but does on Gecko, for getting the "open" property, so if you set `document.domain` before this line, the get of "open" would fail in Gecko).

The only security checks in the specs I'm aware of are the "perform a security check" bits in IDL and the internal methods of WindowProxy and Location objects.

Oh, and as for the main topic of this issue: what is the point of the check in `doc.open`?  The point is that `doc.open` will change the URL of `doc` to that of "the responsible document of the entry settings object", in https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-document-open step 23.  To prevent confusion about URLs that do not match origins, we want to ensure that the origin continues to match the URL.  But we don't want to _mutate_ origins either, so we check up front that the origin of `doc` matches that of "the responsible document of the entry settings object".  That's what step 4 is about.

Note that "the responsible document of the entry settings object" may well not be same origin-domain with the actual _caller_ of `open()` or the document `open()` is being called on, in all browsers including Gecko.  A simple example: script is entered in window A, calls a function in window B, the function in window B sets document.domain and then calls `open`.  At this point the "entry settings" thing is A, the caller of `open` is B, A need no longer be same origin-domain with B (even in Gecko).  B does have to be same origin-domain in Gecko with the document that `open()` is being called on, of course.

One other note: I would have no objection to tightening the security check here to require that the document being `open`ed is both same-origin _and_ same origin-domain with "the responsible document of the entry settings object" if people want that.

I should also note that Chrome and WebKit do _some_ sort of security checks here.  I'm just not sure which ones.  For example, http://web.mit.edu/bzbarsky/www/testcases/document/document-open-domains.html throws from every single test.  But maybe they're checking same origin-domain or something?

I should note that  http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/saved/4851 (cited above) doesn't make sense to me: in that testcase both windows are same-origin _and_ same origin-domain at all times, so there's just no security check issue, right?  Hence no exceptions in any browsers.

@bzbarsky can you clarify what case should throw when you said "On the other hand, Chrome does not seem to perform any security check from inside the IDL operation at all, so the spec also does not define Chrome's security model. ;)"

> Per the current specs as written, in @jeisinger's testcase, when you call docOpen you land in the steps
> defined in step 2 of https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#dfn-create-operation-function. Step 2.1.2.3 says:

I read the spec that creating docOpen runs the "create an operation function" steps, but later calling it doesn't run those steps again.

The "create an operation" steps are run at global creation time.  They create the JS Function object.

Step 2 of "create an operation" defines the variable _steps_ to be a list of steps, but doesn't _run_ them or anything.  Then step 3 passes this variable to CreateBuiltinFunction.  That lands you at <https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-createbuiltinfunction>.  Per step 3 of that algorithm the result is a function that "when called performs the action described by _steps_".

ok, I think this boils down to https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#integration-with-idl step 2 (IsPlatformObjectSameOrigin) not being implemented in blink (nor is that easily implementable)
soo... the conclusion is that "same origin-domain" is the right behavior but tests are hard?

Conclusion for which?

`document.open` needs to do an actual "same origin" check.  See https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2288#issuecomment-277066898
